title: Accelerating Influence Function Estimation for Large Language Models: A Practical Design

problem.claim: Existing influence-function methods are impractical for large language models because of prohibitive storage and I/O costs.

gap.claim: Prior approaches suffer from a fidelity gap caused by coarse curvature approximations and an I/O bottleneck caused by materializing per-example gradients.

contributions.claim: StructInf is a structure-aware influence-estimation framework based on system-algorithm co-design.
StructInf uses an adaptive block-diagonal damped empirical Fisher surrogate with quadratically convergent Newton--Schulz iterations for curvature estimation.
StructInf uses streaming computation to remove per-example gradient storage, reduce space complexity from O(N • d) to O(d), and address distributed split-view bias through gradient calibration.

author_reported_evidence.claim: StructInf enables real-time data selection during training compared with prior methods requiring hours of pre-computation or TB-scale storage.
Across GLUE and instruction-tuning benchmarks, StructInf achieves up to +26% AUC on MRPC and an average 7× speedup for 7B-scale models.
The authors report that high-fidelity influence analysis is practical on a single RTX 4090.

narrative_sequence.summary: Influence functions are principled for tracing predictions to training data, but existing methods are impractical for LLMs.
The main barriers are inaccurate curvature approximations and infeasible per-example gradient storage.
StructInf combines curvature modeling, streaming computation, and distributed gradient calibration.
The authors evaluate StructInf against baseline methods using comprehensive experiments.
The authors report faster, lower-storage, and higher-AUC influence analysis for the stated benchmarks and hardware setting.

source_observation.claim: The framework jointly addresses curvature fidelity, gradient-storage cost, and distributed curvature coordination.

interpretation.claim: For large-scale influence analysis, algorithmic accuracy and systems constraints can be coupled design requirements.

application.claim: Design scalable data-attribution methods by co-optimizing numerical approximations, memory usage, and distributed statistics.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the reported trade-offs generalize beyond the stated LoRA-tuned LLM, benchmarks, model scale, and hardware settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the baseline methods, full experimental protocol, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not provide implementation details sufficient to assess reproducibility.
The abstract does not quantify communication costs or define the scope of the stated high-fidelity guarantee.
